items.prompt: What do attackers usually look for first?
choices: The strongest lock to break
The cheapest gap to use
The newest feature to test
items.explanation: They want the most result for the least effort.

items.prompt: What is an attack surface?
choices: The one server holding all data
The list of staff with admin rights
Every place input can enter or leave
items.explanation: It is every endpoint, field, header and dependency an outsider can reach.

items.prompt: Which of these is a cheap gap?
choices: An id in a URL with no owner check
A password stored with a strong hash
A connection protected by TLS
items.explanation: Changing a number costs nothing, and nothing stops it.

items.prompt: Is the OWASP Top 10 a single named flaw?
choices: Yes, one flaw in databases
Yes, one flaw in browsers
No, it is a list of categories
items.explanation: It names kinds of mistake that recur in real incidents.

items.prompt: Do most incidents need a brand-new unknown flaw?
choices: No, most use ordinary known mistakes
Yes, nearly all of them depend on one
Yes, because known flaws always get fixed fast
items.explanation: Missing checks, old routes and stale libraries are enough.

items.prompt: One door is hardened. What does an attacker do next?
choices: Give up on the whole app for good
Try another door that is weaker
Try the hardened door again, harder
items.explanation: Doors are independent, so a weaker one is simply used instead.

items.prompt: What is the OWASP list based on?
choices: One expert's personal opinion
Categories seen in real incidents
Which tools are most popular
items.explanation: It is re-ranked periodically from real-world data.

items.prompt: Which describes an attacker's incentive?
choices: Most result for least effort
Most elegant technique available
Most famous target in the world
items.explanation: Cheap and reliable beats clever.

items.prompt: A team spends a quarter strengthening password storage. An attacker then reads other customers' invoices by changing a number in a URL. Why did the quarter's work not stop it?
choices: Password storage was still weak, so the attacker cracked the stored hashes first and then browsed freely
The invoice route was protected by an outdated encryption algorithm that the attacker was able to break
It closed one category, while the attacker used a different one with no check at all
Attackers will always find a way around stored-password protection whatever strength it has
items.explanation: Hardening password storage closes cryptographic failures. The invoice route fell to broken access control, a separate door.
items.reference:
How an attacker picks a way in
list every place input enters (the attack surface)
try cheap guesses in each, skip what resists
strong crypto is costly, so rarely first
the weakest category gets used
Why: attackers follow the cheapest gap, not the most impressive lock.
items.learnMore:
The cheapest gap

An attacker maps the attack surface and tries inexpensive guesses: a changed id, strange text, an old route. Whatever resists is skipped, so hardening one door does not close the others.

Common mistake

Assuming attackers aim at the strongest defense. They aim at the weakest one they can find.
items.reflection: Think of a place you protect well and a place you ignore. Which one would someone with no special skill try first?

items.prompt: A review finds four things. Which would an attacker most likely use first?
choices: A forgotten staging route that answers with no sign-in
A password database hashed with a slow, strong setting chosen for safety
A site served over TLS with a modern, well-reviewed configuration
A session token signed with a long random key held in a vault
items.explanation: The forgotten route needs no skill, while the other three would each be costly to attack.

Attackers cannot tell which defense is the strongest
Encryption is never worth funding at any amount at all
Attackers are paid for results, so they take the weakest category rather than the strongest

choices: That the whole app is secure against every one of the ten categories on the list
Only that the transport protection held; other categories were not shown safe
That the attack surface is small enough that it can safely be ignored from now on
That access control and injection were also tested and held up under attack too

items.prompt: Broken access control belongs to which family?
choices: Who may do what
Protecting data
Design and visibility
items.explanation: It asks whether a person is allowed to do a specific thing.

items.prompt: Injection belongs to which family?
choices: Setup and upkeep of the system
Input that becomes a command
Protecting data in storage
items.explanation: The input is run as an instruction instead of kept as data.

items.prompt: SSRF belongs to which family?
choices: Who may do what here
Input that becomes a command
Design and visibility of abuse
items.explanation: A supplied address makes the server act as it was told.

items.prompt: Security misconfiguration belongs to which family?
choices: Setup and upkeep
Who may do what
Protecting sensitive data
items.explanation: The settings are unsafe, not the logic.

items.prompt: Logging and monitoring failures belong to which family?
choices: Setup and upkeep
Design and visibility
Input that becomes a command
items.explanation: It is about noticing abuse when it happens.

items.prompt: Cryptographic failures belong to which family?
choices: Who may do what
Setup and upkeep
Protecting data
items.explanation: They concern data being unprotected where it sits or travels.

items.prompt: How many categories are in each family here?
choices: Two
One
Four
items.explanation: Five families of two make the ten categories.

items.prompt: Is this grouping an official OWASP structure?
choices: Yes, it is OWASP's official layout
Yes, since the most recent revision
No, it is a memory aid for this unit
items.explanation: OWASP publishes a ranked list, and the families are this unit's own layer.

items.prompt: An app fetches whatever web address a user pastes, from the server. Which family does that mistake sit in, and why?
choices: Who may do what, because users lack permission to paste addresses at all
Input that becomes a command, because supplied text decides what the server does
Protecting data, because the pasted address is sent without any encryption
Setup and upkeep, because the fetch feature is switched on by default in the framework
items.explanation: The supplied address controls where the server connects, which is input turned into an instruction.
items.reference:
Five families, two categories each
who may do what: access control, authentication
input becomes a command: injection, SSRF
protecting data: cryptographic, integrity
setup and upkeep: misconfiguration, outdated parts
design and visibility: insecure design, logging
Why: grouping by the question each category answers makes ten names easier to hold.
items.learnMore:
Grouping the ten

Each family answers one question: who may do what, did input stay data, is data protected, is the setup safe and current, and did we plan for abuse and watch for it. The grouping is a memory aid for this unit, not an official OWASP structure.

Common mistake

Treating the families as official OWASP sections. They are a study aid.

items.prompt: A sign-in form allows unlimited password guesses, and nobody is alerted when thousands arrive. Which two families do these gaps sit in?
choices: Protecting data, and setup and upkeep
Input that becomes a command, and protecting data
Setup and upkeep, and who may do what
Who may do what, and design and visibility
items.explanation: Unlimited guesses weaken authentication, and no alerting is a monitoring gap.

Who has admin rights to the dashboard and its reports?

items.prompt: Hashing and encryption both sit in which category?
choices: Injection of commands
Cryptographic failures
Insecure design choices
items.explanation: Both protect data using cryptography.

items.prompt: Login and session handling belong to which category?
choices: Server-side request forgery of internal addresses
Security logging and monitoring failures
Identification and authentication failures
items.explanation: They answer who the user is.

items.prompt: Does strong cryptography cover the other categories?
choices: No, each category needs its own work
Yes, if it is applied everywhere
Yes, but only for databases
items.explanation: The categories are independent.

items.prompt: One category is excellent. Where does the attacker go next?
choices: Back to the excellent one
Nowhere, the attack ends
To the weakest category
items.explanation: They follow the cheapest remaining gap.

items.prompt: At most how many of ten categories do the crypto and login units cover?
choices: Two
Seven
Ten
items.explanation: Cryptographic failures and authentication failures.

items.prompt: How are the categories best pictured?
choices: As one long chain of links
As independent doors
As a single overall score
items.explanation: Closing one leaves the others as open as before.

items.prompt: Which unit goes deeper on permission models?
choices: Hashing
Authorization models
Symmetric and asymmetric encryption
items.explanation: Authorization models covers who may do what.

items.prompt: Where does extra effort reduce risk the most?
choices: On the weakest category
On the strongest category
On the most visible category
items.explanation: The weakest door is where the attacker will go.

items.prompt: Plan A doubles effort on encryption, already strong. Plan B adds a basic check to each of the eight categories with no coverage. Which lowers risk more, and why?
choices: Plan A, because encryption is the category that attackers target most often
Plan A, because strong categories give compounding protection to the whole app
Plan B, because it removes the open doors the attacker would move to
Neither, because risk cannot be lowered by adding checks
items.explanation: Doubling an already strong category leaves every other door as open as before.
items.reference:
What the other units close
hashing, encryption, TLS: cryptographic failures (1 of 10)
login and sessions: authentication failures (1 of 10)
together: at most 2 of 10 categories
eight categories remain open
Why: categories are independent doors, so strength behind one says nothing about the rest.
items.learnMore:
Independent doors

Cryptography and login units close two categories. The other eight, including access control, injection and misconfiguration, need their own work, and an attacker simply uses whichever is open.

Common mistake

Reading progress on one category as progress on security as a whole.
items.reflection: Think of something you have secured well. What nearby thing did that effort leave exactly as exposed as before?

items.prompt: An auditor states that all cryptographic controls pass, so the app is secure. What is the best response?

Agreed, because cryptography is the foundation that every other category rests upon
Agreed, provided the same controls are shown to pass again next year
Disagree, because cryptographic controls cannot be audited in any meaningful way
items.explanation: A pass in one category is not a claim about the others.

A stronger setting for password hashing
An inventory of every route that the application exposes today
A review of who may read each kind of record, written down
items.explanation: Password hashing protects stored passwords and has no effect on whether an endpoint checks ownership.

items.prompt: Security misconfiguration means what?
choices: Setup is unsafe though the code is fine
A function somewhere has a logic bug in it
A password was guessed by a stranger
items.explanation: The risk comes from how the system is set up.

items.prompt: Which is a misconfiguration?
choices: A bug in a sorting function
A default password never changed
A slow database query
items.explanation: Nothing is wrong in the logic, only in the setting.

items.prompt: Outdated components means what?
choices: A function with no automated tests at all
A library with a known public flaw
A page with old styling and fonts
items.explanation: The flaw is documented and a fix exists.

items.prompt: What closes the outdated components gap?
choices: Track dependencies and update them
Rewrite every dependency yourself instead
Hide the version number from visitors
items.explanation: You cannot fix what you do not know you ship.

items.prompt: What is a logging and monitoring failure?
choices: A password is too short to be safe
A breach happens and nobody notices
A route answers too slowly for users
items.explanation: Nothing records or flags the abuse.

items.prompt: What is insecure design?
choices: A typo in a variable name that nobody noticed
A missing semicolon at the end of a line
Rules that allow abuse even if code is right
items.explanation: The flaw is in the plan, not in a line.

items.prompt: What is an integrity failure?
choices: Trusting an update without checking
Choosing a long password for every account
Closing an unused port on the firewall host
items.explanation: The code or data may have been swapped on the way.

items.prompt: Can code review alone catch most setup gaps?
choices: Always, provided the review is done carefully
Yes, if the reviewers are experienced
Rarely, because they live outside the code
items.explanation: Settings, versions and old routes are not in the diff.

items.prompt: A debug page is still reachable on the live site. Which category is this, and what is the fix?
choices: Insecure design; redesign the debug page's database schema from scratch
Security misconfiguration; remove or disable what the product does not need
Injection; escape every piece of text that the debug page displays
Logging failure; record every single visit made to the debug page
items.explanation: Nothing in the logic is wrong. The setting is, and the fix is to switch off what is unused.
items.reference:
Gaps that need no code bug
misconfiguration: debug page or default password left on
outdated components: a library with a known flaw
integrity: an update trusted without checking the source
logging: a breach nobody notices
insecure design: rules that allow abuse
Why: they are fixed by habits (review setup, track dependencies, watch logs), not by editing one function.
items.learnMore:
Setup and upkeep

A running system is code plus its settings, dependencies and surroundings, and all three change after the code is written. Each gap here is closed by a routine, not by a one-line patch.

Common mistake

Assuming a clean code review means the running system is safe.
items.reflection: Think of a tool you installed once and never reviewed. Which default or old version might still be sitting there?

items.prompt: A library has a public flaw, and the team says it never calls the broken function. What is the sound conclusion?
choices: It is safe, because functions that nobody calls are never able to run
It is safe, because the flaw only becomes public after a fix exists
It is unsafe only if the library happens to be open source software
It is not proven safe, since the flaw may be reachable through other paths
items.explanation: Reachability inside a dependency is hard to prove, so the dependable habit is to update.

Cryptographic failure, because the guesses are not encrypted in transit
items.explanation: The code does what it was designed to do, so the flaw is in the design.

items.prompt: An app downloads and applies an update without checking its signature or checksum. What is missing?
choices: Encryption of the update file after it has been applied to the host
A longer, random file name for the downloaded update package
Verification of where the update came from before trusting it
Logging that records the moment at which the update ran
items.explanation: Without verification a swapped file is trusted, which is an integrity failure.

items.prompt: What does injection mean?
choices: Data being stored in a table
Input being run as a command
A database query being slow
items.explanation: The input changes what the interpreter does.

items.prompt: Which is the structural fix for injection in queries?
choices: Stripping quote marks
Hiding error messages
Parameterized queries
items.explanation: They keep value and command apart.

items.prompt: In a parameterized query, the value travels as what?
choices: Data only
Part of the command
A comment
items.explanation: The database never parses it as syntax.

items.prompt: Why are joined strings dangerous?
choices: They are always slower to run on big tables
They use far more memory per request
The database cannot tell data from code
items.explanation: It receives one finished sentence.

items.prompt: Does an apostrophe in O'Brien break a parameterized query?
choices: No, it stays plain data
Yes, it ends the command
Yes, unless escaped by hand
items.explanation: Only the value channel carries it.

items.prompt: A filter that strips quote marks is what?
choices: A complete fix for the whole problem
A guess at dangerous spellings
The same thing as parameterizing
items.explanation: Attackers can use spellings the filter did not list.

items.prompt: The textbook input ' OR '1'='1 shows what?
choices: A database crash from too many rows
Input changing the command shape
A network delay caused by retries
items.explanation: The extra text became part of the command.

items.prompt: Which can injection also target beyond a database?
choices: A shell command
A font file
A screen colour
items.explanation: Any interpreter fed joined text is exposed.

items.prompt: Which code is open to injection?
choices: A query whose shape is fixed and that takes the term as a separate value
A query with no user input at all and a constant filter inside it
A query built by joining the search term into the command text
A stored command that receives the term through a placeholder
items.explanation: Only the joined version lets the term change the command's structure.
items.reference:
Joined text versus two channels
joined: command + user text become one string
parameterized: fixed shape + separate value
value is data only, never structure
O'Brien is just a name, not a quote
Why: parameters make the code/data boundary structural, so there is nothing to filter.
items.learnMore:
Injection and parameters

When user text is joined into a command, the interpreter cannot tell where the developer's words end. Sending the value separately removes that ambiguity. Filtering characters tries to enumerate every dangerous spelling and always risks missing one.

Common mistake

Believing a stripped quote or blocked word is equal to a structural fix.
items.reflection: Think of a form letter with a blank for a name. What if the name written in the blank were an instruction to the reader?

items.prompt: A developer blocks quotes and the word OR in input. An attacker still gets through using an alternate spelling. What is the right conclusion?
choices: Blocklists chase spellings, so keep input out of the command structure
The blocklist needed more words added to it before it was released
The database should hide its error messages from the attacker
Input length should be limited to ten characters per field
items.explanation: Filtering guesses at dangerous forms. Parameters remove the ambiguity structurally.

items.prompt: A report page lets users choose which column to sort by. Why can a parameter not simply carry the column name?
choices: Column names are longer than ordinary values, so they always exceed the length limit that applies to values
Placeholders only ever accept numbers, never any kind of text value
Sorting by a user's choice is never safe in any circumstance
Placeholders carry values, not structure, so check the name against a fixed list
items.explanation: The column is part of the command's shape. An allowlist of known names keeps it controlled.

items.prompt: A value was stored safely through a parameterized insert. Later, another query joins that stored value into its command. What went wrong?
choices: The first insert should have used joined strings as well, for consistency
Data from your own database was trusted, though a user originally supplied it
Stored values can never be read back safely by any later query
The database wrongly encrypted the value when it was saved
items.explanation: Origin matters: a value stays untrusted wherever it is later stored or read.
items.reference:
Joined text versus two channels
joined: command + user text become one string
parameterized: fixed shape + separate value
value is data only, never structure
O'Brien is just a name, not a quote
Why: parameters make the code/data boundary structural, so there is nothing to filter.
items.learnMore:
Injection and parameters

When user text is joined into a command, the interpreter cannot tell where the developer's words end. Sending the value separately removes that ambiguity. Filtering characters tries to enumerate every dangerous spelling and always risks missing one.

Common mistake

Believing a stripped quote or blocked word is equal to a structural fix.

items.prompt: What is SSRF?
choices: A server fetching an attacker's chosen address
A browser running a script an attacker planted
A user guessing a password over and over
items.explanation: The server makes the request for the attacker.

items.prompt: Why can the server reach what the attacker cannot?
choices: It has a faster connection
It sits inside the network
It has a better browser
items.explanation: Internal addresses are reachable only from inside.

items.prompt: What is 169.254.169.254 commonly?
choices: A public search engine
A cloud metadata address
A database port number
items.explanation: It is link-local and can hand out temporary credentials.

items.prompt: What does a protocol check allow?
choices: Only http and https
Every scheme
Only file
items.explanation: It blocks file: and other non-web schemes.

items.prompt: What is stronger than a blocklist?
choices: A longer and longer blocklist of bad hosts
An allowlist of needed destinations
No check at all on the address
items.explanation: Only known-good places are reachable.

items.prompt: Which feature risks SSRF?
choices: Rendering a static page of text
Hashing a password before storing it safely
A link preview fetching a pasted address
items.explanation: It makes a server-side request to a supplied place.

items.prompt: When should the address be checked?
choices: After resolving the name
Only as it was typed in
Never, since names are safe
items.explanation: A name can point to a private address.

items.prompt: Which is a private range?
choices: Any address ending .com
items.explanation: Private ranges are reserved for internal use.

items.prompt: A filter rejects addresses that start with 10. or 192.168. An attacker supplies a normal-looking name that resolves to a 10.x address. Why does it pass?
choices: The filter only ever works on addresses that start with HTTPS
The filter reads the typed text, not the address the name leads to
Names are never checked by any filter that has been written
10.x addresses are not actually private ones, and are reachable from anywhere
items.explanation: Resolve first, then check the address you will connect to.
items.reference:
The server as a messenger
attacker outside the network cannot reach internal addresses
the server inside can
a user-supplied address makes it fetch for them
check protocol, resolved address, prefer an allowlist
Why: SSRF lends the attacker the server's position inside the network.
items.learnMore:
Server-side request forgery

A feature that fetches a user-supplied address from the server can be pointed at private destinations, including cloud metadata at 169.254.169.254. Check the protocol and the address the name resolves to, and prefer an allowlist of needed destinations.

Common mistake

Checking the typed text instead of the resolved address.

items.prompt: Which design most reduces SSRF risk for a feature that tests customer webhooks?
choices: Block the word localhost in the typed address and the typed host
Limit the size of the response to the first kilobyte only
Require the user to be signed in before they can submit
Allow only approved hostnames and check the resolved address before connecting
items.explanation: Allowlisting plus a resolved-address check controls where the server may go.

items.prompt: Implement `isLoggedIn(session)`: return `true` when the session exists and has a `userId`, otherwise `false`.

tests.expr: expect(isLoggedIn(null)).toBe(false)
expect(isLoggedIn({})).toBe(false)
expect(isLoggedIn({ userId: 7 })).toBe(true)

items.explanation: Authentication only asks whether a real user is attached to the request, so both a missing session and a session without `userId` mean no.

items.prompt: Implement `isOwner(invoice, session)`: return `true` when the invoice's `ownerId` equals the session's `userId`.

tests.expr: expect(isOwner({ ownerId: 7 }, { userId: 7 })).toBe(true)
expect(isOwner({ ownerId: 7 }, { userId: 8 })).toBe(false)

items.explanation: Authorization compares the record's owner to the requester. This one comparison is what a valid session alone never gives you.

items.prompt: Implement `findInvoice(invoices, id)`: return the invoice with that `id`, or `null` if there is none.

tests.expr: expect(findInvoice([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], 2)).toEqual({ id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 })
expect(findInvoice([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], 99)).toBe(null)

items.explanation: Looking the record up is the step before any ownership check, and a missing record needs its own explicit answer.

items.prompt: Implement `ownedBy(invoices, userId)`: return an array of the `id` of every invoice owned by that user, in order.

tests.expr: expect(ownedBy([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], 7)).toEqual([1, 3])
expect(ownedBy([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], 99)).toEqual([])

items.explanation: Filtering by owner is how a list endpoint applies the ownership rule: it selects only the caller's rows.

items.prompt: Implement `canRead(session, invoice)`: return `true` only when the session has a `userId` and it matches the invoice's `ownerId`.

tests.expr: expect(canRead({ userId: 7 }, { ownerId: 7 })).toBe(true)
expect(canRead({ userId: 8 }, { ownerId: 7 })).toBe(false)
expect(canRead(null, { ownerId: 7 })).toBe(false)

items.explanation: Both questions must pass: someone is signed in, and that someone owns the record.

items.prompt: Implement `countOwned(invoices, userId)`: return how many invoices that user owns.

tests.expr: expect(countOwned([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], 7)).toBe(2)
expect(countOwned([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], 99)).toBe(0)

items.explanation: Counting is the same owner filter as listing, ending in a length instead of the rows.

items.prompt: Implement `totalOwned(invoices, userId)`: return the sum of `total` over invoices owned by that user.

tests.expr: expect(totalOwned([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], 7)).toBe(31)
expect(totalOwned([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], 8)).toBe(5)
expect(totalOwned([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], 99)).toBe(0)

items.explanation: Only the caller's own rows contribute: 20 + 11 = 31 for user 7, and nothing leaks in from user 8's invoice.

items.prompt: Implement `accessStatus(session, invoice)`: return `"unauthenticated"` if there is no `userId`, `"forbidden"` if the user is not the owner, otherwise `"ok"`.

tests.expr: expect(accessStatus(null, { ownerId: 7 })).toBe("unauthenticated")
expect(accessStatus({ userId: 8 }, { ownerId: 7 })).toBe("forbidden")
expect(accessStatus({ userId: 7 }, { ownerId: 7 })).toBe("ok")

items.explanation: The order matters: first who you are, then whether the record is yours.

items.prompt: Implement `getInvoice(invoices, session, id)`. Throw `new Error("not authenticated")` when there is no `userId`, `new Error("not found")` when no invoice has that id, `new Error("forbidden")` when the invoice belongs to someone else. Otherwise return the invoice.

tests.expr: expect((() => { try { return getInvoice([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], null, 1); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })()).toBe("not authenticated")

expect((() => { try { return getInvoice([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 7 }, 99); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })()).toBe("not found")

expect((() => { try { return getInvoice([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 7 }, 2); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })()).toBe("forbidden")

expect((() => { try { return getInvoice([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 7 }, 3); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })().id).toBe(3)

items.explanation: The checks run in order: user, record, owner. Skipping the last comparison is the exact gap behind an IDOR, so every signed-in user could read every invoice.
items.reference:
Authentication versus authorization
authentication: is there a real signed-in user?
authorization: does this user own this record?
no record to compare (list): filter by owner
one wrong order of checks changes what leaks
Why: the ownership comparison is the check a valid session never provides.
items.learnMore:
Writing the ownership check

A permission check has an order: confirm there is a user, find the record, then compare its owner. Each failure gets its own answer, and which answer you give can itself reveal whether a record exists.

Common mistake

Returning the record after checking only that a session exists.
items.reflection: Think of a library desk that checks your card at the door. What else must the clerk check before handing you a specific book that is on hold for someone else?

items.prompt: Implement `listInvoices(invoices, session)`. Throw `new Error("not authenticated")` without a `userId`. Otherwise return only the invoices the user owns, in their original order.

tests.expr: expect((() => { try { return listInvoices([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], null); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })()).toBe("not authenticated")
expect(listInvoices([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 7 }).map((i) => i.id)).toEqual([1, 3])
expect(listInvoices([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 99 })).toEqual([])

items.explanation: A list has no single record to compare, so the owner rule is applied while selecting the rows. A signed-in user with no invoices gets an empty list, not an error.

items.prompt: Implement `deleteInvoice(invoices, session, id)`. Throw `new Error("not authenticated")` without a `userId`, `new Error("not found")` for a missing id, and `new Error("forbidden")` unless the user owns the invoice or `session.role` is `"admin"`. Return a new array without the invoice and leave the original array unchanged.

tests.expr: expect((() => { try { return deleteInvoice([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], null, 1); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })()).toBe("not authenticated")

expect((() => { try { return deleteInvoice([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 7 }, 2); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })()).toBe("forbidden")
expect(deleteInvoice([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 1, role: "admin" }, 2).map((i) => i.id)).toEqual([1, 3])
expect(deleteInvoice([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 7 }, 1).map((i) => i.id)).toEqual([2, 3])

expect((() => { const list = [{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }]; deleteInvoice(list, { userId: 7 }, 1); return list.length; })()).toBe(3)

items.explanation: A destructive action uses the same ownership rule as a read, with a deliberate exception for an admin role. Returning a new array keeps the caller's data safe from accidental mutation.

items.prompt: `getInvoiceHidden(invoices, session, id)` should behave like a read endpoint that does not reveal which ids exist. Throw `new Error("not authenticated")` without a `userId`. For a missing invoice OR an invoice owned by someone else, throw the same `new Error("not found")`. Otherwise return the invoice. The starter leaks by answering "forbidden" for other people's invoices; fix it.

tests.expr: expect((() => { try { return getInvoiceHidden([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], null, 1); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })()).toBe("not authenticated")

expect((() => { try { return getInvoiceHidden([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 7 }, 99); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })()).toBe("not found")

expect((() => { try { return getInvoiceHidden([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 7 }, 2); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })()).toBe("not found")

expect((() => { try { return getInvoiceHidden([{ id: 1, ownerId: 7, total: 20 }, { id: 2, ownerId: 8, total: 5 }, { id: 3, ownerId: 7, total: 11 }], { userId: 7 }, 1); } catch (e) { return e.message; } })().id).toBe(1)

items.explanation: Answering forbidden confirms the record exists, which lets a guesser map valid ids. Giving the same answer for missing and not-yours reveals nothing. The ownership comparison itself is unchanged.
